data.title: Eli Lilly joins Huntington’s race on $725m LoQus23 takeover
data.description:
Eli Lilly is back on the dealmaking bandwagon with an agreement to acquire British biotech LoQus23 Therapeutics and its Huntington’s disease therapy as the race to market the first treatment in this indication continues. 

By outlaying up to $725m in upfront and milestone payments, Lilly will absorb the rights to LoQus23’s pipeline of preclinical small molecule candidates, which the biotech has designed to slow the expansion of triplet repeats in relevant genetic diseases like fatal neurodegenerative disorder Huntington’s and neuromuscular condition myotonic dystrophy type 1. 

At the heart of this deal is LoQus23’s lead candidate LQT-23, an oral, indirect selective inhibitor of MutS Homolog 3 (MSH3) – a protein that is believed to be involved in Huntington’s disease progression and is intimately involved in DNA mismatch repair. According to LoQus23, the potentially disease-modifying drug has already demonstrated its Huntington’s potential in preclinical studies, with LQT-23 blocking somatic expansion in relevant cell and animal models. 

With positive preclinical data in the bag, LoQus23 hopes to submit a clinical trial application for LQT-23 in “the near future”, which could take the drug one step closer to an indication with significant unmet needs. Currently, researchers estimate that 75,000 people across the US, UK and Europe are impacted by Huntington’s disease, which currently has no approved therapies specifically for it and is generally fatal around 15-20 years after onset.  

An approved product could be on the cards next year, however. Dutch biotech UniQure submitted its gene therapy, AMT-130 for review by US regulators after navigating a tumultuous regulatory road for the drug. UniQure has the most clinically advanced disease-modifying asset for Huntington’s disease. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has set a target action date of 1 May 2027.  

Lineage Cell Therapeutics also recently secured a place in a race to the Huntington’s market by acquiring Neuroairmid Therapeutics and its clinical-stage neural network-building therapy last week 

While LoQus23 is now under Lilly’s wing, the drugmaker was not the first pharma giant to see promise in LoQus23’s approach, as Novartis’ venture arm also backed the company in both its seed and Series A round. 

According to LoQus23’s CEO, Dr David Reynolds, Lilly takeover brings its ambitions of creating a disease-modifying therapy for Huntington’s disease a step closer to reality. 

“Lilly has the neuroscience track record, scale, and expertise to accelerate LQT-23 into and through the clinic; we look forward to working with Lilly to deliver on the potential of LQT-23 for patients,” Reynolds commented. 

This acquisition marks another high-profile bid from Lilly, which has been on a broad-ranging dealmaking streak in 2026. The big pharma’s double-down on dealmaking comes as sales of its weight loss drug tirzepatide continue to explode – with the franchise alone outperforming several big pharma companies in Q3. Most recently, the company outlaid $1.5bn to acquire haematology-focused biotech Calytrix Bio and inked a $5.9bn cancer licensing pact with Stipple Bio on the same day. 

The deal also comes as the British biotech sector records a stellar year. There have now been several high-profile exits for British biotechs, including Centessa Pharmaceuticals, Silence Therapeutics, Myricx Bio, and Dark Blue Therapeutics.  

The financing scene has also seen success, with UK-based artificial intelligence (AI)-backed Isomorphic Labs securing $5bn in the largest ever biotech funding round in history. Arecent report from the BioIndustry Association (BIA) finding that the UK is likely on track to post its best year since 2021 for biotech venture capital (VC) acquisition.

data.title: Horus Pharma and Epitech Group agree global adelmidrol deal
data.description:
French company Horus Pharma has entered into an exclusive global licensing agreement with Italian biopharmaceutical firm Epitech Group to develop and commercialise adelmidrol.

The arrangement covers applications in both human ophthalmology and periocular dermatology.

Under the deal, Horus Pharma assumes responsibility for managing the marketing and development of new ophthalmic formulations containing the compound.

Adelmidrol is an ALIAmide family molecule developed by Epitech Group, a company that specialises in neuro-inflammation research. The transaction is intended to evaluate new methods of addressing unmet medical needs in ocular care.

The initiative comes amid an ageing global population, a rising incidence of chronic conditions, and an increasing complexity of ocular surface disorders.

Through the collaboration, the two companies intend to explore the clinical utility of the molecule to address these challenges.

Epitech Group CEO Raffaella della Valle said: “We’re delighted to join forces with Horus Pharma, whose recognised ophthalmology expertise and commitment to scientific innovation make it an ideal partner.

“This partnership will enable us to explore prospects for this molecule in the field of eye health, on a global scale.”

Horus Pharma CEO Claude Claret said: “The work that we’ve carried out has further strengthened our interest in the potential of adelmidrol in terms of eye health and the opportunities it could unlock.

“We’re particularly pleased to combine our expertise with that of Epitech Group. We want to continue exploring this molecule and helping to come up with new solutions to benefit patients and healthcare professionals alike.”

The development programme draws on research originating from Rita Levi-Montalcini, who initially discovered the ALIA mechanism. Epitech Group has spent more than 30 years researching ALIAmides and their function in physiological regulatory processes.

Horus Pharma contributes more than two decades of ophthalmology sector experience, an international commercial presence, and internal research and development capabilities to the project.

data.title: FDA approves Novo’s Sogroya for paediatric Turner syndrome
data.description:
The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved Novo Nordisk’s once-weekly Sogroya (somapacitan-beco) injection to treat growth failure in patients aged 2.5 years and above with Turner syndrome.

Turner syndrome is a chromosomal condition in females caused by a missing or altered X chromosome, frequently resulting in short stature, fertility issues, heart defects, and kidney disorders.

The human growth hormone analogue is administered subcutaneously in doses of 5mg, 10mg, or 15mg.

The regulatory clearance was based on findings from the REAL8 clinical trial programme, an open-label, active-comparator, Phase III basket study (NCT05330325). REAL8 evaluated 105 treatment-naïve, pre-pubertal patients aged 2.5 to 10 years with Turner syndrome. They were randomised into a 2:1 ratio to receive either 0.24mg/kg per week of Sogroya or 0.05mg/kg per day of somatropin.

At week 52, patients receiving Sogroya achieved an annualised height velocity of 8.9cm per year, compared to 9.7cm per year for those on daily somatropin, representing an estimated treatment difference of -0.8cm per year. Change in the annualised height standard deviation score from baseline was 0.77 for the once-weekly therapy and 0.86 for the daily comparator.

The somatropin dose used in the study was lower than the maximum US-approved paediatric dosage of 0.067mg/kg per day for Turner syndrome.

The most frequent adverse reactions, occurring in at least 10% of participants treated with Sogroya during the initial 52-week evaluation period were diarrhoea, ear infection, injection site reaction, nasopharyngitis, pyrexia, respiratory tract infection, and vomiting. Patients enrolled in the trial are currently continuing in a two-year safety extension phase.

Novo rare disease group vice-president Colleen Silk said: “For children with Turner Syndrome, growth hormone treatment can be part of everyday life for years. How they experience that treatment matters. A once-weekly option represents a meaningful advancement in how we support growth in children with Turner Syndrome, reducing the number of injections throughout that journey.

“This approval reflects our commitment to advancing the treatment experience for children and their families. With Sogroya now approved across five distinct growth-related disorders, we are building on Novo’s decades of innovation with a clear purpose: to help meet children’s growth needs in ways that recognise the lives they and their caregivers lead.”

In addition to Turner syndrome, Sogroya holds US approval for adults with growth hormone deficiency.

In April this year, Novo Nordisk partnered with OpenAI to expedite its drug development efforts, as the Danish pharma looks to fend off stiff competition from obesity market rival Eli Lilly.

data.title: MSD and Isomorphic join forces to develop oncology drugs
data.description:
MSD (Merck & Co) has forged a partnership with British artificial intelligence (AI)-powered biotech Isomorphic Labs, which will see the pair collaborate on cancer drug development as the former looks to offset the looming patent cliff of its blockbuster checkpoint inhibitor Keytruda (pembrolizumab). 

Though precise details were not disclosed, MSD did note that the duo will band together to discover therapeutic small molecules against a specific oncology target of strategic importance.  

To further this mission, Isomorphic will feed MSD’s proprietary data sets into its drug design engine, IsoDDE, which will help the biotech to design and deliver molecular designs for new drug candidates faster than traditionally possible. Isomorphic will also take the lead on performing computer-based simulations to predict how effective a drug may be – potentially boosting the likelihood of a candidate’s success in the clinic. 

In exchange for an undisclosed upfront payment and potential research, development, regulatory and commercial milestones, as well as tiered royalties on potential net sales, MSD will secure the rights to any resulting fruits of this collaboration – with the US pharma giant taking the helm on preclinical and clinical development, as well as the manufacturing and commercialisation of any drugs created. 

Additionally, Isomorphic has the choice to co-fund development activities around resulting drugs to secure elevated royalties on therapies developed in tandem with MSD. 

MSD and Isomorphic ink this partnership a little after the latter made history by snagging the largest Series C raise in biotech history – securing $5bn to advance its range of AI-developed candidates across several modalities and therapeutic areas closer to the clinic. 

It also comes as MSD faces significant revenue losses through the impending patent expiry of its best-selling asset, Keytruda, which pulled in $8.6bn across its intravenous and subcutaneous formulations (Keytruda QLEX) in Q3 2026. 

With Keytruda revenues set to dip, MSD is now looking to the potential of several late-stage assets – including the Moderna co-developed cancer vaccine intismeran autogene, which analysts are touting as a potentially strong commercial opportunity following the drug’s late-stage win in adjuvant melanoma. 

Analysts are also taking a growing interest in antibody-drug conjugate (ADC), sacituzumab tirumotecan (sac-TMT), which has demonstrated notable promise across a range of cancers thus far in late-stage trials. The latest win for the TROP2-directed therapy was in a type of stomach cancer, with the drug having met its primary endpoint of overall survival (OS) in the third-line-plus metastatic gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma setting. 

MSD is bolstering its early-stage pipeline to seek more mid-to-long-term growth, with the company having inked a $2.1bn cancer licensing deal with Chinese biotech SciBrunch Therapeutics focused on its KRAS(ON) inhibitor in September 2026. The pharma giant pens this agreement as KRAS-targeting therapies create a buzz in the sector, with Revolution Medicines’ next-generation RAS inhibitor Rasonque (daraxonrasib) securing landmark US and European approvals in pancreatic cancer during August and November, respectively.

data.title: Novartis CEO leans on surge of pipeline readouts to quell growth fears
data.description:
Faced with a steep cliff of patent expirations for some of its key commercial assets, Novartis has shone a light on its pipeline as it seeks to ease investor fears regarding its growth into the next decade.

The Swiss drugmaker said it expects more than 35 readouts that could enable drug submissions through 2031. Candidates in development span oncology, immunology, neuroscience, and cardiovascular-renal-metabolic. Ten of the assets in late-stage development have multi-billion-dollar peak sales guidance, according to Novartis.

The pipeline overview was revealed to investors in London on 19 November as part of a wider unveiling of the company’s long-term growth trajectory. Novartis projects net sales to grow at a 5% compound annual rate between 2026 and 2031. The guidance marks a slight dip from a previous range of 5-6% from 2025 to 2030.

Novartis is bracing for significant drops in revenue for some of its marketed drugs. Key amongst these is breast cancer treatment Kisqali (ribociclib), which generated $4.78bn in global sales in 2025. GlobalData’s Pharma Intelligence Center predicts peak revenue of nearly $11bn in 2030, before a drop to $6.9bn in 2032 – the year market exclusivity is expected to end in the US.

GlobalData is the parent company of Pharmaceutical Technology.

Along with its potentially blockbuster-filled pipeline, Novartis also pointed to current commercial brands that it expects will fill revenue gaps in the coming years. The company raised peak sales guidance for three key brands – multiple sclerosis treatment Kesimpta (ofatumumab), blood cancer drug Scemblix (asciminib), and lipid-lowering injection Leqvio (inclisiran). Kesimpta is expected to generate the most from these at $8bn, though Novartis did not provide a year.

Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan said: “In 2026 we expect to grow through the largest loss-of-exclusivity impact in our history.”

Citi analysts called the investor event “upbeat”, highlighting that the sales guidance was above Visible Alpha consensus.  

“[Novartis has] the building blocks to achieve mid-single-digit growth post-2031 despite major loss of exclusivities,” they said in a research note.

They added: “We see the new above-consensus outlooks as positive but expect market to remain sceptical of post-2031 growth pending further pipeline data.”

Alongside in-house R&D, Novartis has sought external innovation. In June, the company outlaid up to $1.9bn in a cancer partnership with Antares Therapeutics. However, Novartis’ corporate structure recently faced scrutiny after trial setbacks rocked investor confidence in the company’s M&A strategy.

Among these was del-desiran’s failure in the Phase III HARBOR study (NCT06411288), evaluating the drug as a treatment in the rare muscle-wasting disease myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1). Del-desiran was the flagship product in Novartis’ $12bn acquisition of Avidity Biosciences, which closed in February 2026. Following the readout, a major Novartis shareholder called for a shake-up of the drugmaker’s board to improve corporate governance, though Narasimhan was not blamed.

data.title: Sanofi rumoured to be eyeing high-profile Insmed takeover
data.description:
Sanofi is reportedly mulling a takeover bid for respiratory disease-focused biotech Insmed as the company approaches an M&A-heavy dealmaking strategy under its new CEO Belén Garijo. 

As per Bloomberg, which first reported the news, the French pharmaceutical giant is currently in talks with its advisers, which could lead to a deal that sources say may become the largest of its kind since Pfizer’s $43bn Seagen acquisition in 2023. 

Insmed declined to provide comment, while Sanofi did not immediately respond when approached by Pharmaceutical Technology. 

If the deal goes through, Sanofi would absorb the rights to Insmed’s portfolio of respiratory medicines, which includes non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis (NCFB) therapy, Brinsupri (brensocatib) and refractory Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) lung disease drug, Arikayce (amikacin liposome inhalation suspension). The company would also secure access to Insmed’s pipeline, which includes a range of clinical and preclinical medicines for a variety of lung conditions, such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). 

According to head biotech equity research analyst at William Blair, Matt Phipps, Sanofi has been seen as a “rational fit” for Insmed due to their overlapping respiratory franchises. 

“We believe it particularly makes sense in light of the commercial push into COPD with the recent Dupixent approval,” Phipps commented in a research note. However, he did question whether Sanofi has the capacity for this deal, and the price that Insmed would be willing to sell at.  

The reported deal comes as Sanofi looks to fortify its pipeline and portfolio amid the looming patent expiry of its blockbuster respiratory drug Dupixent (dupilumab), which is slated to lose its US market exclusivity in 2031. In Q3 2026, Dupixent’s sales ballooned by nearly 35% to reach €5.7bn ($6.2bn). 

At the time of the Q3 results debut, Sanofi’s CFO, Francois Roger, noted that the French pharma is increasingly eyeing larger deals centred around late-stage investigational or marketed products – primarily in the areas in which it is known, including vaccines, immunology and rare diseases.  

According to a research note from Jefferies’ European pharma and biotech lead, Michael Leuchten, these areas of focus are a “good strategic fit” for Sanofi, and M&A will play a key role in bolstering Sanofi’s outlook as Dupixent’s loss of exclusivity nears.  

This change in tack comes as Garijo – prior CEO of Merck KGaA – looks to set Sanofi up for future growth. She has also promised investors that she will speed up decision-making within the company.  

Garijo took the helm at Sanofi in May after prior CEO Paul Hudson was ousted following a string of high-profile clinical trial failures.

data.title: Merz Therapeutics: Staying focused while scaling a global neuroscience business
data.description:
The global burden of neurological disease continues to create significant opportunities for pharmaceutical innovation. An estimated 1.2bn people worldwide were living with migraine in 2021, while Parkinson’s disease affected approximately 11.8m people globally. Meanwhile, China’s growing biopharmaceutical sector is reshaping the international licensing landscape, with Chinese biotechnology companies attracting increasing interest from global pharmaceutical developers.

Against this backdrop, Frankfurt-headquartered Merz Therapeutics is pursuing an expansion strategy to double the size of its business by the end of the decade. Rather than diversifying across therapeutic areas, the German drugmaker is concentrating investment in neuroscience, with an increasing focus on neurological pain, including migraine and neuropathic conditions.

The strategy combines internal clinical development with external innovation through acquisitions, licensing agreements and international partnerships. China is emerging as an important part of this approach, not only as a substantial commercial market but also as a source of clinical development opportunities and innovative biotechnology assets.

In conversation with Pharmaceutical Technology at the FT Global Pharma & Biotech Summit in London in November, Merz Therapeutics’ CEO Stefan König explains how the company intends to build scale while maintaining its specialist focus, where it sees opportunities in the evolving neuroscience market, and why pricing, reimbursement and patient access remain significant challenges for the pharmaceutical industry.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Catherine Longworth (CL): You joined Merz Therapeutics in 2023 with a mandate to accelerate the business. What was the ambition when you arrived, and how has the strategy evolved?

Stefan König (SK): It is important to understand Merz Therapeutics in the context of the wider Merz Group. The group comprises three businesses: Merz Therapeutics, Merz Aesthetics and Merz Life Care, which operates primarily in consumer healthcare and over-the-counter pharmaceuticals.

As a family-owned business, the group wanted to ensure that it was not disproportionately exposed to any one of these businesses. The ambition was therefore to bring Merz Therapeutics to a comparable scale to its sister businesses and accelerate its contribution to the group.

Since I joined, we have doubled the size of the organisation and expect to double it again by the end of the decade. That growth will be driven by two principal engines: our own clinical development programmes and external innovation through business development, including acquisitions and licensing.

We have also invested in building an organisation that can support this expansion. That includes a scalable operating model, a matrix structure and additional capabilities in launch and commercial excellence. We are also deploying artificial intelligence (AI) across both commercial operations and research and development.

Importantly, we have advanced several clinical programmes into Phase II and Phase III over the past three years. These programmes are beginning to feature much more prominently in our longer-term business planning.

CL: Merz has established itself as a specialist neuroscience company. Do you see opportunities to broaden the therapeutic focus as the business grows?

SK: Our strategy is to expand through greater depth in neuroscience rather than diversification into other therapeutic areas.

We have a clearly defined footprint covering Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, movement disorders and, increasingly, neurological pain conditions such as migraine and polyneuropathies.

There are adjacent rare and orphan diseases that fit within these areas, but we do not intend to move outside our neuroscience focus. As a mid-sized pharmaceutical company, we need to be disciplined about where we invest and where we believe we can make the greatest difference.

There may be some geographical expansion, although we already have a very global business. Approximately 45% of our revenues come from the US, while a substantial proportion of our European revenues is generated through our own affiliates.

We currently operate in China through distribution partners, so establishing a more direct presence there is a possibility. We may also consider selected opportunities elsewhere in Asia. However, I do not envisage a major geographical transformation of the business. Our priority is to build a stronger portfolio within neuroscience.

CL: How do you differentiate Merz Therapeutics in a competitive neuroscience market increasingly attracting investment from larger pharmaceutical companies?

SK: Large pharmaceutical companies are less present in some of the specialist areas in which we operate, partly because the individual disease markets can be relatively small.

There is also a difference in the types of innovation being pursued. Larger pharmaceutical companies have historically invested heavily in disease-modifying therapies, whereas a significant proportion of our portfolio comprises symptomatic treatments.

Unfortunately, we have seen a number of high-profile failures in late-stage development programmes targeting disease modification. That reinforces the importance of continuing to provide effective symptomatic therapies for patients who need treatment today.

This creates an important role for specialist, mid-sized pharmaceutical companies. We can concentrate on specific neurological conditions and develop treatments that address unmet needs which may not always attract the same level of investment from larger players.

CL: China is becoming an increasingly important player in global pharmaceutical development. What opportunities do you see for Merz Therapeutics in the market?

SK: I see three distinct areas of opportunity. First, China represents a substantial commercial market with a significant patient population and considerable medical need. We have recently signed a co-development agreement for one of our Parkinson’s disease products. Given the scale of the Parkinson’s population in China, bringing innovation to these patients is an important part of our international strategy.

However, China requires a specific development and commercial approach. Companies need either an appropriate local presence or strong strategic partners who understand the market.

Second, China offers opportunities to improve the efficiency of clinical development. Clinical trials can be conducted competitively in terms of both cost and timelines. If we want to accelerate global development programmes and improve their cost efficiency, we need appropriate representation of Chinese patients in international clinical trials.

I am not suggesting that programmes should be conducted exclusively in China. Rather, we need to ensure that Chinese patients are adequately represented in global clinical development.

Third, and increasingly importantly, China is becoming a source of pharmaceutical innovation. Historically, the country has been recognised primarily as a manufacturing centre. That remains important, but I believe its future value to the global pharmaceutical industry will increasingly come from biopharmaceutical innovation.

For Merz, this creates opportunities to acquire, license or establish joint ventures with Chinese biotechnology companies. These three dimensions – the commercial market, clinical development and external innovation – underpin our interest in China.

CL: The international licensing environment has become increasingly competitive. What makes an asset or potential partner attractive to Merz?

SK: Ultimately, we are looking for a drug that makes a meaningful difference for patients and demonstrates that it works. We also need an appropriate risk profile, particularly when we are considering clinical-stage assets or development programmes.

But the quality of the asset is only one part of the equation. The partner is equally important. As a family-owned business, we take a long-term perspective. We consider the value that a treatment can bring to patients and healthcare systems, rather than focusing exclusively on short-term commercial returns.

We look for partners who share that philosophy: organisations with a patient-focused approach, a serious long-term commitment and a strong ethical culture.

Trust is fundamental. If you combine an attractive clinical asset with a partner that shares those values, you have the foundations of a successful collaboration.

CL: Beyond China, the wider pharmaceutical industry continues to face challenges in translating clinical innovation into patient access. Where do you see the greatest obstacles?

SK: For a commercial-stage pharmaceutical company such as Merz, the biggest challenge is pricing, reimbursement and the speed of market access.

We have therapies that were launched in the US several years ago and have entered certain European markets more recently. However, we have still not secured access in other parts of Europe because reimbursement discussions can be prolonged and there are often disagreements between companies and payers about the value of innovation.

The situation varies considerably between European countries, making market access a complex and fragmented process.

Whenever we assess a new clinical innovation, we challenge ourselves with a fundamental question: will healthcare systems pay for this treatment, and will patients be able to access it quickly?

Unfortunately, in Europe, the answer is not always straightforward. The US is different. Innovation is generally more readily recognised and rewarded, including incremental improvements rather than only major advances that fundamentally change treatment paradigms.

In China and Japan, the challenges are somewhat different. There is greater regulatory complexity around ensuring that local patients are appropriately represented in global clinical development programmes.

Ultimately, the ability to demonstrate clinical value is only one part of the equation. We also need regulatory approval, reimbursement and effective market access if we are going to translate innovation into meaningful patient benefit.

CL: What would you identify as the most significant strategic decisions since you took over the business?

SK: The first was the introduction of our Pivot for Growth strategy, which established how we intended to accelerate the development of Merz Therapeutics.

The strategy has provided the framework for doubling the size of the organisation and our ambition to double again over the coming years.

The second was advancing a number of clinical-stage programmes as part of that strategy. These programmes are important because they will provide the basis for future portfolio expansion.

We have also made deliberate choices about our organisational structure. We have adopted a matrix, patient-centric and asset-centric operating model designed to support more effective collaboration across the business.

Finally, we have pursued acquisitions of attractive commercial-stage assets. External innovation is an important complement to our internal development programmes and will remain a central part of our growth strategy.

CL: Looking ahead over the next five years, which clinical programmes and milestones will be most important?

SK: We expect to expand further into neurological pain, building on our established positions in movement disorders, Parkinson’s disease and multiple sclerosis.

Migraine is an important opportunity. We have two global Phase III studies running in parallel, with results expected during the coming year. Subject to positive data and the necessary regulatory approvals, we would expect to move towards commercialising the asset and establishing Merz Therapeutics as a player in migraine prevention.

We believe there is considerable unmet clinical need in migraine. Existing treatments can have significant side effects, and not all patients achieve adequate or sustained control of their condition.

Our approach is based on a different innovation profile from some of the treatments introduced in recent years. We hope to demonstrate improvements in efficacy, safety and ease of use through our clinical development programme.

However, migraine is not the only opportunity in neurological pain. We also have a Phase II programme in neuropathic pain, which has recently reported results and was presented at the Global Pain Congress in Bangkok. We believe the data could provide the basis for progressing into Phase III in the near future, potentially across different neuropathic pain indications and patient populations.

These programmes represent an important next step in broadening our neuroscience portfolio while remaining within our core therapeutic focus.

CL: The migraine market has attracted significant interest from pharmaceutical companies and medical technology developers. How do you see the competitive landscape developing, and where do you believe Merz can differentiate itself?

SK: The first point is that there remains substantial unmet need in migraine.

There are many patients who do not respond adequately to existing therapies, and tolerability and ease of use remain important considerations.

We hope our clinical data will demonstrate a differentiated treatment profile, particularly in terms of efficacy, safety and convenience.

The market is also evolving beyond conventional pharmaceutical treatments, with medical devices and neuromodulation technologies contributing to the range of available approaches.

For us, the priority is to demonstrate meaningful clinical differentiation. We need to show that our approach can offer a genuine improvement for patients, rather than simply adding another treatment option to an already competitive market.

CL: Finally, how important will external innovation and partnerships be to Merz Therapeutics over the next phase of its development?

SK: External innovation will remain fundamental to our strategy.

We are primarily focused on drug development rather than early-stage drug discovery. Consequently, we are continuously looking for the right targets, companies and assets, particularly in the later stages of clinical development within neuroscience.

That applies to opportunities in China, but also to biotechnology companies and pharmaceutical partners in other parts of the world.

We want to identify programmes with attractive clinical potential that can complement our existing portfolio and benefit from our development, regulatory and commercial capabilities.

Our ambition is to build a larger, more competitive neuroscience business, and external partnerships will be an essential part of achieving that.

data.title: Recursion CEO details novel Phase III endpoint for rare disease drug
data.description:
Recursion Pharmaceuticals has secured alignment with the FDA on a novel endpoint for its planned Phase III trial of REC-4881, an investigational treatment for familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP).

Speaking at the 2026 Jefferies Global Healthcare Conference in London on 18 November, Recursion’s CEO Najat Khan said the composite endpoint, which includes the excision of 10mm polyps could help capture the clinical benefits of the AI-enabled programme in a disease with a very high unmet need and patient burden and no approved therapies. The composite event-free survival measure is the study’s primary endpoint.

REC-4881 is an oral MEK1/2 inhibitor being developed for FAP, a rare inherited disease caused by loss-of-function mutations in the APC gene. The condition is progressive and leads to the development of hundreds of precancerous polyps throughout the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, putting patients at significant risk of colorectal cancer.

“Polyps that are greater or equal to 10 millimeters are the ones that are known to have high risk of dysplasia and cancer,” Khan said. “It’s hard to remove them. There’s risk of perforation, bleeding, and often also incomplete removal of the polyp,” she added.

According to Khan, incorporating the novel component of polyp excisions into the composite endpoint is particularly important because removing larger polyps is already part of routine FAP treatment paradigm.

The randomised, placebo-controlled trial is expected to enrol approximately 200 adults with FAP who have previously undergone colectomy or proctocolectomy and is on track to begin in the second half of 2027.

FAP affects more than 50,000 people across the US and five major European markets, according to Recursion’s CEO. Patients typically undergo surgery to remove the colon to reduce their risk of colorectal cancer. However, polyps can continue developing in the remaining rectum, ileal pouch and upper GI tract, requiring repeated endoscopic surveillance and further interventions, highlighting the substantial burden of the disease.

“These patients are ‘going under’ for endoscopies and polyp removals, multiple times a year. So this is a highly, highly invasive, life-altering, and intensive disease,” Khan said.

Recursion’s AI capabilities

Recursion is seeking to demonstrate that its AI platform can repeatedly identify novel drug targets and develop differentiated medicines, with REC-4881’s planned Phase III trial representing a significant example.

Recursion is also using its artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities to inform the registrational study design. Khan said the company used natural history data and scraped approximately 256,000 physician notes covering around 1,000 patients to better understand disease progression and how FAP is currently managed.

The programme forms part of Recursion’s wider effort to demonstrate the clinical potential of its AI-enabled drug discovery platform, which has also produced the first-in-class oncology candidate REC-1245.

The company has additionally advanced partnered programmes with Sanofi and Roche.

Phase II data bolster pivotal trial plans

Recursion’s Phase III plans for REC-4881 follow updated results from its ongoing Phase Ib/II TUPELO study (NCT05552755), which demonstrated reductions in polyp burden across both the upper and lower GI tract.

Data presented earlier this month showed that 87% of patients experienced a reduction in total polyp burden after 12 weeks of treatment with REC-4881, with a median reduction of 47%. Approximately one-third of patients achieved reductions of at least 65%.

The effects also appeared durable, with 85% of evaluable patients remaining below their baseline polyp burden 12 weeks after stopping treatment. “Even when the patients are followed for three months off drug, most of the reduction is sustained,” Khan said.

Khan said the results were particularly encouraging in the upper GI tract, where removing polyps can be challenging because of the thin intestinal lining and associated risks of bleeding and perforation. The executive highlighted one patient case whose number of upper GI polyps measuring more than 5mm fell from 96 to just one following treatment. “That patient with over 96 polyps would have met the criteria for surgery. And with one polyp, they don’t meet the criteria for surgery,” Khan said. The company believes reducing polyp burden could translate into fewer surgical interventions, although this will need to be demonstrated in the pivotal study.

data.title: Geopolitical pressures and greater buyer selectivity hamper M&A deal closure rates
data.description:
While M&A appetite has been strong in 2026, deals are increasingly thwarted by valuation gaps, geopolitical uncertainty and greater selectivity among buyers.

Reflecting on the year, industry experts at the 2026 Jefferies Global Healthcare Conference in London, taking place 16–19 November pointed to declining successful deal closure rates across the sector.

The current geopolitical backdrop has introduced additional complexity into the dealmaking process. Head of healthcare at Downing Investment Management Mark Gross observed that there has been a “stop-start” dynamic throughout the year, where changeable macro environments have delayed or derailed decision-making.

This sentiment was echoed by Hardik Madlani, managing director of Healthcare Investment Banking at Jefferies, who expressed hope that 2027 may offer more stability. “[In the] last two years, we have seen wars, we have seen inflation, we have seen interest rates,” he said.

Dissecting the deal execution pattern further, Madlani characterised 2026 as a “year of two halves.” While corporate deal activity, particularly in the first half of year, has been strong, private equity has been subdued and selective, he explained.  

Gross offered additional insight into the private sector, arguing that while there is “no shortage of capital,” investors are taking a “more discerning” approach to decision-making.

In addition, Gross partly attributed a high number of aborted processes in 2026 to a mismatch between value expectations of sellers and what buyers are prepared to pay following due diligence.

Meanwhile, biopharma dealmaking is also trending towards greater selectivity. “I don’t think we are in a market where people just buy for growth,” said Madlani. Companies are now thinking more carefully about the strategic fit and quality of acquisitions, he added.

While big pharma will continue to replenish its pipeline, companies need substantial “conviction” in the assets they are purchasing so will focus on innovation and capabilities, added Aisling Zarraga, partner at the law firm Linklaters.

Europe tells a different story

While there has been robust global biopharma M&A activity in 2026, the European perspective is “very different,” according to Arun Krishnan, vice president of corporate development at Norgine.

Uncertainty around drug pricing, fueled by introduction of the Most Favored Nation (MFN) policy in the US has had significant implications for deal volumes and value, he added.

Krishnan explained that companies are less willing to part with European rights for innovative assets in fear of the potential impact on an assets value in the US, leading to a marked decrease in licensing deals.

Looking ahead to 2027, Krishnan postulated that a mid-sized EU-focused biopharma company like Norgine will need to either “go global” or “get creative” to find pockets of “MFN-proof” deal opportunities. He highlighted rare diseases assets as exempt from MFN and vaccines as a therapeutic class with less disparity between US and EU pricing.

data.title: Ellipses Pharma plots London listing that could end British biotech IPO drought
data.description:
London-based Ellipses Pharma said it might conduct an initial public offering (IPO) on home soil, an announcement that could mark the end for one of the longest ever dry spells for biotech listings in Britain.

Ellipses, which is developing treatments for various types of cancer, said it has signed an agreement in principle with special purpose acquisition company (SPAC) Wolfram Resources.

Ellipses and Wolfram are targeting a deal completion by early 2027, though caveated that there is no guarantee the proposed transaction will proceed.

SPACs are already listed shell companies that acquire private companies to take them public on the stock market. This method used to be considerably more common five years ago given their higher safety, though fell out of fashion after many companies with speculative growth trajectories failed to reach valuations.

With a low enthusiasm for listings on the London Stock Exchange (LSE) this year, Ellipses has so far decided to go down the SPAC route. The biotech’s non-binding Memorandum of Understanding with Wolfram will see a reverse takeover, with the latter acquiring Ellipses’ whole share capital.

There has not been a single biotech that listed on the LSE in 2026, marking one of the quietest windows in the sector’s history in the capital. Experts have also highlighted the challenging investment climate across the wider European capital markets scene.

In stark contrast, the US IPO scene has exploded in 2026. There have been around 30 biotech and pharma listings on the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) and the Nasdaq, marking the strongest year since the 2020/2021 boom.

Targeting a listing on home soil marks a positive step for the UK biotech sector, which has seen numerous funding and exit successes this year. This week, Isomorphic Labs raised $5bn in the largest ever biotech Series C round.

Professor Sir Chris Evans, Ellipses CEO, said: “Our company has been focused resolutely on the development of promising drug candidates and the progress made with our pipeline, including encouraging results from our clinical trials for both EP0031 and EP0062, which indicates that this is now the optimal time to move towards a public listing.

The renowned British biotech entrepreneur added: “We also see our main market listing as a shot in the arm for the UK Life Sciences sector which has a great scientific pedigree.”
